title: Naam: the Name
hookLine: Naam is more than a word; it is the presence of the One, remembered until it fills you

lines: A NAME READ OFF A LIST.
A NAME THAT CARRIES A PRESENCE.
cards: A name gets said in a lot of ways. Read off a list at the dentist's office, it's flat, just a label. Shouted across a parking lot, it's a signal.
And then there's the way someone who loves you says it, maybe a parent when you were small, or a grandparent who's gone now. That voice didn't only identify you. It held you.
Same name, completely different thing. Said a certain way, a name carries a whole presence with it. Sikhs have a word for the Name of the One, and they mean it that second way.

teach.b: Today's word is naam. Literally, name. But in the Granth, naam is far more than a word for God.
It's the presence of the One, running through everything, which a person can remember until it fills them. You've heard it from the very beginning.
The Mool Mantar calls the One Satnam: truth is the Name. Pauri 4 of the Japji says: in the ambrosial early hours, reflect on the true Name.
And Pauri 19 says it boldly: jetaa keetaa tetaa naaou.
As much as has been made, that much is the Name. Vin naavai naahee ko thaaou: without the Name, there's no place at all. So naam isn't a label stuck onto creation.
Creation is where the Name shows up, which is why the Granth keeps coming back to it.
Sikh teaching sums up Guru Nanak's way in three simple pillars, and naam japo, remember the Name, is one of them, alongside honest work and sharing with others.

Naam simran, remembering the Name, can mean repeating Waheguru, singing hymns, or simply holding the One in mind while you chop onions or drive to work. And yesterday's riddle, the disease with its own cure?
Sikh teachers point to naam as that medicine.
When the Name fills you, there's less room for the I-me. It isn't pushed out by force. It's more like a room filling with light: the shadows don't lose a fight; they just aren't there anymore.

how: Many Sikhs practice naam simran by repeating Waheguru, singing kirtan, or holding the One in mind through the day; naam japo, remembering the Name, is taught alongside kirat karo, honest work, and vand chhako, sharing.

games.q: you've caught haumai, the I-me, crowding the room. what do Sikh teachers point to as the medicine?
o: naam: remembering the Name until it fills you.
games.why: when the Name fills you, there's less room for the I-me, like shadows gone when a room fills with light.

practice: No task, no counting: if you'd like, let the word Waheguru rise silently on a slow breath in, and settle on the breath out.
If that word isn't yours, simply rest in the quiet, the way you'd sit in a room with someone you love without needing to talk. Let whatever presence you feel fill the space, slowly, like light.
